parts.problem_md: Explain **one **advantage to an employer of using a person specification.
parts.solution_md:
A person specification lists the skills, qualifications and personal qualities needed for a job, showing which are essential and which are just desirable **[1]**. This gives an employer a clear, consistent set of criteria to compare every candidate against, which makes it easier to spot the most suitable person for the role **[1]**. It also means the employer is less likely to rely on personal opinion or guesswork when choosing between applicants, reducing the risk of hiring the wrong person **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded up to 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A person specification sets out the skills, qualifications, experience, and personal qualities required for a role, distinguishing between essential and desirable attributes
> - It informs potential applicants about the type of person the business is looking for, helping them to self-select before applying.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - By making the requirements of the role clear, unsuitable candidates are less likely to apply, reducing the volume of applications the employer must review and shortening the recruitment process — saving both time and money
> - Having a clear list of essential and desirable criteria allows the employer to assess all candidates consistently and objectively, making it easier to identify the most suitable person for the role and reducing the risk of a poor hiring decision
> - A well-written person specification can also attract higher-quality applicants, as candidates who closely match the criteria are more likely to apply, improving the overall standard of the candidate pool
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problem_md: Explain **two **advantages to a business of using induction training.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage of induction training is that new employees quickly learn what is expected of them **[1]**, including the business's rules, procedures, and health and safety requirements. This means they can make an effective start to their role and are less likely to make costly mistakes in the early stages of employment **[1]**

A second advantage is that induction training helps new employees feel welcomed and confident in their new workplace **[1]**. When employees feel settled and supported from the start, they are more likely to be motivated and to stay with the business **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded up to 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Induction training familiarises new employees with the business's procedures, expectations, and working environment.
> - It helps new employees understand the structure of the business and their role within it.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Knowing what is expected and how to carry out their role correctly from the start means new employees are less likely to make errors, reducing wasted time and resources and helping the business maintain consistent standards of output or customer service
> - Feeling welcomed and settled increases new employees' motivation and sense of belonging, making them more likely to remain with the business and reducing the costs associated with high labour turnover
> - Understanding future promotion routes can motivate employees to work hard and develop their skills, benefiting the business through a more capable and committed workforce over time
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ravi's Sportswear (RS)**
> 
> Ravi founded RS in country J eight years ago. The business designs and sells sportswear and running shoes. RS employs 25 full-time staff and sells its products through its own website and a small number of selected sports retailers across country J.
> 
> Ravi has recently launched a new range of women's sportswear, targeting the growing women's fitness market in country J. He has invested heavily in digital promotion and influencer partnerships to promote the new range, which has led to high marketing expenditure in the first quarter of 2024.
> 
> RS currently uses on-the-job training to develop all new employees. Ravi is considering whether to switch to off-the-job training, which would be more expensive in the short term but would develop employees' skills more systematically.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows RS's cash flow forecast for the first three months of 2024.
> 
> **Table 1.1: RS cash flow forecast (January–March 2024)**
> 
> |   | January (\$000) | February (\$000) | March (\$000) |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Cash inflows | 45 | 28 | 52 |
> | Cash outflows |   |   |   |
> | Cost of goods sold | 22 | 18 | 25 |
> | Wages | 12 | 12 | 12 |
> | Marketing | 15 | 5 | 5 |
> | **Total outflows** | **49** | **35** | **42** |
> | **Net cash flow** | **−4** | **−7** |   |
> | Opening balance | 12 | 8 |   |
> | **Closing balance** | **8** |   |   |

Evaluate whether RS should introduce off-the-job training rather than continuing to use on-the-job training for new employees.
parts.solution_md:
On-the-job training means employees learn while doing their normal work, supervised by an experienced colleague. Off-the-job training means employees attend external courses or workshops away from the workplace **[K]**

One reason RS should switch to off-the-job training is that it develops skills to a higher standard **[K]**. RS operates in specialist areas such as digital marketing and product design, where external trainers have more current knowledge than internal supervisors **[Ap]**. RS has recently invested heavily in influencer partnerships and digital promotion for its women's range **[Ap]**, so employees with formally trained digital marketing skills could manage these campaigns more effectively, potentially increasing sales revenue **[An]**. Off-the-job training also reduces the risk of employees learning bad habits from colleagues, helping to maintain consistent standards across the team **[An]**

However, RS is already under significant cash flow pressure. In January 2024, net cash flow is −\$4,000 and in February it is −\$7,000, mainly due to the \$15,000 marketing spend on the new range **[Ap]**. Paying external training fees and losing the productivity of employees **[K]** while they are away from their roles would make this pressure worse. With only 25 staff, RS cannot easily cover the absence of employees during training without affecting day-to-day service and operations at an already demanding time **[An]**

Overall, a full switch to off-the-job training is not the right decision for RS right now **[E]**. While the long-term benefits are clear, especially for specialist roles in digital marketing and product design **[Ap]**, the short-term cost is too high given the current negative cash flow. Ravi should continue with on-the-job training for most roles in the short term, but introduce targeted off-the-job training for key specialist employees from March 2024 onwards, when net cash flow turns positive at +\$10,000 **[Ap]** and the business is in a stronger financial position to absorb the cost **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> **Knowledge and application**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **4** | - Shows understanding of two points in context |
> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one point in context |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two points |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one point |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two points in context |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one point in context |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two points |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one point |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - On-the-job training: employees learn skills while doing their normal work, supervised by an experienced colleague; e.g. coaching, mentoring, job shadowing
> - Off-the-job training: employees receive training away from the workplace through external providers; e.g. formal courses, workshops, professional qualifications
> - RS employs only 25 full-time staff and already has negative net cash flow in January (−\$4,000) and February (−\$7,000) 2024 due to the marketing spend on the women's range - adding the cost of external training fees and lost productivity would increase financial pressure on a small business with limited resources
> - Off-the-job training delivered by specialist external providers can develop skills in areas such as digital marketing and product design to a higher standard than internal supervisors can - it also reduces the risk of new employees picking up poor habits from colleagues and ensures consistent skill standards across the team
> - On-the-job training allows employees to remain productive while learning; off-the-job training requires employees to be absent from their roles, which is difficult to manage in a business of only 25 staff and could affect service quality and operations during the women's range launch
> - The case for off-the-job training is strongest for specialist roles such as digital marketing and product design, where external expertise adds the most value; for more routine roles, on-the-job training may be perfectly adequate - a phased approach targeting key roles may offer the best balance
> - Timing is a key consideration: RS's cash flow is negative in January and February but improves to +\$10,000 in March; Ravi may be better placed to introduce off-the-job training once cash flow stabilises rather than during a period or financial pressure
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> For high-mark "Evaluate" questions, always structure your answer around both sides of the argument before reaching a final judgement. Many students lose marks by only discussing the benefits of one option without considering the drawbacks or the alternative.
> 
> Make sure you use the case study throughout your answer — refer specifically to RS's cash flow figures, the size of the workforce (25 staff), and the current pressures from the women's range launch. Generic answers about training that could apply to any business will not score well on AO2 (Application).
> 
> A strong evaluation does not simply state "RS should do X." Instead, it considers the circumstances under which one approach might be better than the other. For example, you might argue that a blended or phased approach is most appropriate given RS's current financial position. This kind of nuanced, conditional judgement is what examiners look for at the top level of AO4.
> 
> Avoid spending too long defining on-the-job and off-the-job training — only 2 marks are available for knowledge. The bulk of your answer should focus on analysis and evaluation in context.

**[12 marks]**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** effect on a business of a high rate of labour turnover.
parts.solution_md:
A high rate of labour turnover means the business must frequently recruit and train replacement staff, which is expensive and time-consuming **[1]**. While new employees are being inducted and learning their roles, they are unlikely to work as efficiently as the experienced staff they replaced, which can reduce productivity and lower the quality of output or customer service **[1]**. Over time, these additional costs and disruptions can significantly reduce the business's profit margins **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> A high rate of labour turnover means employees leave the business frequently and must be replaced, increasing recruitment, selection, and training costs
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Higher costs - the business must repeatedly spend money on advertising vacancies, interviewing candidates, and training new recruits; while replacements are being inducted, productivity is likely to fall, adding further to costs and potentially reducing output or customer satisfaction
> - Loss of skills and experience - when experienced employees leave they take their knowledge with them, which can reduce the quality of work and place extra pressure on remaining staff who may need to cover additional responsibilities until a replacement is found
> - Impact on morale - remaining employees may feel unsettled or overburdened if colleagues frequently leave, leading to lower motivation and potentially causing further staff to leave, making the problem worse over time
> - Disruption to operations - constant changes in staffing make it difficult to maintain consistent standards, which can damage customer relationships and harm the business's reputation
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you do more than simply state an effect - the command word "explain" means you need to develop your point. For example, do not just write "higher costs"; instead, explain why costs increase and what impact this has on the business. A good approach is to identify the effect, then link it to a consequence such as reduced productivity, lower quality of output or decreased employee morale. Many students lose marks by listing multiple effects rather than fully developing one - focus on depth, not breadth.

**[3 marks]**

**Extract:**

Cash4Trash (C4T) C4T is located in the capital city of country A in Africa. This private limited company was started six years ago by Andy and Kris, who both had experience working for a large international charity. C4T is a social enterprise, initially financed by international charities and a grant from the government of country A. The government also provided land to C4T for its factory. C4T’s corporate objectives include two social objectives which are to: • improve the environment of the city • provide jobs for the unemployed. C4T collects and cleans all types of recyclable materials that have been discarded as trash (rubbish). The clean materials are then used to create products for sale, such as bags made from woven plastic. A local artist volunteers her services to help with product designs. C4T has grown and now manufactures a range of products from recycled materials, including bags and jewellery. Cases for laptops and smartphones are currently its most popular products. Products are sold to local people and tourists in its shop next to the factory. C4T also sells via its website. C4T employs 90 people in its factory, who were previously unemployed. It runs training courses for 16 to 18 year olds to teach them basic skills. All profit is re-invested to expand and improve the business. C4T has won awards for being a sustainable social enterprise. Operations problems Factory employees work in teams and are rewarded with bonus payments if they exceed targets. Each team collects materials and other resources needed for production from a central store. However, sometimes this store runs out of resources, halting production. Products are checked for quality at the end of the production process and many are rejected and faults have to be corrected. Employees have been trained to specialise in one task within one team. Andy and Kris feel that time and resources are being wasted and would like to reorganise the factory and improve employee flexibility. Marketing Marketing products made from recycled materials can be a major challenge in country A. Many consumers think these products are of inferior quality. However, C4T’s brand image is strong. Its products have featured in premium magazines and on websites aimed at consumers who are ‘socially responsible’. Kris works hard to keep the C4T website up-to-date and maintain its social media presence, as part of the company’s attempt to establish good customer relationships. An ambitious new idea Plastic water bottles have become a real environmental problem over recent years as more are bought and thrown away when empty. Kris is planning to introduce a new type of product. He thinks there is a market for durable, reusable plastic drinking bottles. These will be made from recycled plastic and marketed as souvenirs for tourists. Demand will be highest during holiday periods. parts.problem_md:
‘Human Resource Management is the most important department in any large manufacturing business.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solution_md:
Human Resource Management (HRM) is the department responsible for planning, recruiting, developing, and retaining a business's workforce **[K]**. In a large manufacturing business, the quality and efficiency of output depends heavily on having skilled, motivated employees in every area **[K]**, giving HRM a strong claim to being the most important department **[E]** The case for HRM being most important rests on its unique cross-departmental role **[K]**. Unlike other departments that focus on a specific function, HRM supports every other department by ensuring each has the right people with the right skills. In a large manufacturer, this includes production line workers, quality control engineers, procurement specialists, and senior managers **[Ap]**. If any of these roles are filled poorly, the consequences spread across the whole business. Poorly recruited or undertrained production workers will make more errors, waste more materials, and work more slowly, reducing output and damaging the business's reputation for quality **[An]** HRM also manages ongoing training **[K]** to ensure employees keep pace with evolving manufacturing technology, maintaining productivity over time **[Ap]**. High labour turnover is particularly costly in manufacturing, where technical experience matters greatly; effective HRM reduces turnover and preserves the operational knowledge that keeps production running efficiently **[An]** However, other departments make an equally strong case. The Operations department carries out the core purpose of the business - producing goods - and without efficient production processes, skilled recruitment alone will not generate revenue **[Ap] [An]**. Finance ensures the business has working capital to pay wages, buy raw materials, and invest in equipment; without it, the business may fail regardless of the quality of its workforce **[An]**. Marketing identifies customer needs and drives sales, generating the revenue that funds everything else. In practice, all departments depend on each other: HRM cannot recruit without Finance's budget; Production cannot operate without the workers HRM provides; and Marketing cannot sell goods that Production has not made **[An]** Overall, while HRM is undeniably important, it is an overstatement to call it the most important department in all large manufacturers **[E]**. Its unique value lies in underpinning every other department - no function can operate well without the right people - but this influence is indirect. HRM does not produce goods, generate sales, or manage cash flow **[Ap]**. Its relative importance also depends on the context: in a highly labour-intensive manufacturer where skilled workers are scarce, HRM may be the critical limiting factor **[E]**; in a heavily automated factory, production technology and engineering may matter more **[Ap] [E]**. parts.problem_md: Explain **one **type of training that a business may use.
parts.solution_md:
On-the-job training involves employees learning new skills while carrying out their normal work duties, usually by watching or working alongside an experienced colleague **[1]**. For example, a new employee at a restaurant might be shown by a senior member of staff how to prepare food correctly and follow hygiene procedures **[1]**. This approach is cost-effective for the business because no specialist venue is needed, and the training is directly relevant to the tasks the employee will carry out every day **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Induction training
> - On-the-job training
> - Off-the-job training
> - On-line training
> - Video training
> - Shadowing/mentoring training.
> 
> **AO2 Application **
> 
> - Induction training - given to new employees to introduce them to the business; covers health and safety procedures, the layout of the premises, key colleagues, and business rules and expectations, helping new recruits settle in quickly and make an effective start
> - On-the-job training - employees learn by watching or working alongside experienced colleagues in the workplace; it is cost-effective as no external venue is needed, and the skills learned are directly relevant to the employee's role
> - Off-the-job training - employees attend a course or training programme away from the workplace, delivered by a specialist provider; this can introduce new skills and ideas that employees bring back to the business, though it can be more expensive and takes staff away from their duties
> - Online training - employees complete training using computer software at a time and place that suits them; this is flexible and relatively low-cost, making it useful for delivering induction or skills updates to large numbers of staff
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.solution_md:
Workforce planning means ensuring PC has the right number of workers with the right skills to meet its business objectives **[K]**. Bill, the HR manager in country X, must consider several important factors before finalising the plan

One key factor is the 15% labour cost reduction set by Head Office. PC employs 468 people in country X and labour is its biggest expense there **[Ap]**, so this target represents a large cut. Bill could achieve it by reducing headcount, moving more workers onto flexible contracts, or introducing multi-skilling so fewer specialist staff are needed **[K] [An]**. However, production workers have already shown resistance to learning new skills and to flexible working **[Ap]**. If Bill forces these changes, workers may take industrial action or leave the company, which could increase costs rather than reduce them. This means the workforce plan must carefully assess which approach is most likely to achieve the target without causing disruption **[An]**

A second important factor is the need to maintain consistent production **[K]**. PC already produces 45 million cans per year in country X, which is close to its 50 million capacity limit **[Ap]**. Cutting production staff to save costs could cause output to fall short of demand, leading to stock shortages and damaging PC's reputation in one of its most important markets **[An]**. Any reduction in staffing must therefore be planned so that enough workers remain to meet consumer demand reliably **[E]**

Overall, automation is likely the most important factor in the workforce plan **[E]**. It permanently reduces the need for production workers - lowering labour costs without depending on reluctant workers to multi-skill - while also maintaining output levels **[E]**. Although the upfront investment is high, it offers a long-term solution that protects both the cost target and production capacity **[Ap]**. Bill should recommend phasing in automation gradually while using natural wastage and flexible contracts for new hires, rather than making immediate large-scale redundancies that could harm morale and disrupt production in the short term **[An] [E]**
